Benchmarking Knowledge Boundary for Large Language Models: A Different Perspective on Model Evaluation

Xunjian Yin*, Xu Zhang*, Jie Ruan, Xiaojun Wan

Paper ↗arXiv ↗Code ↗

A wrong answer may reflect the prompt rather than missing knowledge; searching for alternative wording reveals facts a model can answer but a fixed benchmark misses.

01 / The research question

A failed question is not a clean test of ignorance

A factual question can fail because the model lacks the information or because that wording does not elicit it. Conversely, a prompt can produce the desired string without expressing the original question. Measuring a knowledge boundary therefore requires more than increasing answer accuracy. The probe must find accessible knowledge while preserving what was asked and resisting prompts that manufacture apparently correct responses.

Consider the illustrative pair “Which country contains Canberra?” and “Canberra is located in which country?” If only one works, a single template underestimates accessible knowledge. But replacing the question with an instruction to output the target country would not demonstrate knowledge at all. The research problem lies between those cases: search beyond a fixed template without allowing the search to redefine success.

02 / Inside the method

Optimize the question under constraints

PGDC searches in the continuous space of token embeddings, where gradients can suggest changes that make an accepted answer more likely. Its target objective allows the answer to appear after some generated text rather than requiring it at the first output position. When several answer aliases are acceptable, the objective can use the easiest valid alias. This avoids treating one surface form as the only evidence of knowing a fact.

Two additional constraints address the risk of gaming the probe. A semantic loss keeps the candidate close to the original prompt's representation, while another term encourages embeddings to remain near real vocabulary items. During optimization, embeddings sufficiently close to a token are projected back to discrete text. The resulting procedure aims to balance useful search directions with readable, semantically faithful questions.

The known answer is part of this optimization, and the method requires white-box access. It is therefore an evaluation procedure for eliciting a fact whose truth is already available to the researcher. It is not a general question-answering technique that discovers unknown correct answers. This distinction is necessary when interpreting the resulting score as a capacity estimate.

  1. 01

    Define accessible knowledge

    Treat a fact as inside the estimated boundary when at least one meaning-preserving formulation elicits an accepted answer.

  2. 02

    Search constrained prompts

    PGDC optimizes prompt embeddings toward known answers, adds a semantic constraint, and projects suitable embeddings back into discrete text.

  3. 03

    Check the search

    Compare against prompting baselines, test fabricated facts, and have human annotators assess whether optimized questions preserve their meaning.

03 / Reading the evidence

Success needs a negative control

  • 34.43 → 71.36

    PaRaRel success (%)

    For LLaMA2, PGDC elicits more accepted answers than the zero-shot baseline, demonstrating how evaluation changes with prompt search.

  • 83.3%

    Meaning preserved

    Human evaluation of LLaMA2's optimized prompts finds substantial but imperfect semantic preservation; successful elicitation alone does not establish valid knowledge.

On PaRaRel with LLaMA2, PGDC reaches 71.36 compared with 34.43 for zero-shot prompting and 66.95 for the paper's paraphrased few-shot baseline. However, the more diagnostic comparison asks whether a probe can also elicit false targets. In the CFACT counterfactual test, AutoPrompt reaches 88.35 for LLaMA2 while PGDC reaches 3.41. Here the smaller number is desirable: the method should not readily force a false fact into the output.

Semantic preservation is still imperfect. Human assessment of 200 PaRaRel samples reports 83.3% preservation for LLaMA2, so a representation-level constraint cannot certify every rewrite. The reported boundary is an empirical estimate under the available search and validation procedures, not a proof that every knowable fact has been found. The paper's knowledge-focused MMLU evaluation also changes questions into cloze form, so those scores should not be read as standard MMLU scores.

Table 1 (LLaMA2 rows only; transposed so methods are rows). Success rate of eliciting the target answer with LLaMA2 (7B): higher is better on PaRaRel and KAssess (true facts), lower is better on CFACT and ALCUNA (counterfactual or fabricated facts). P- baselines count a fact as elicited if any of its listed paraphrases succeeds; ALCUNA has a single expression per query, so P- and plain baselines coincide there. In the full table (GPT-2, GPT-J, Vicuna, LLaMA2), PGDC is also highest on PaRaRel and KAssess except Vicuna on PaRaRel, where P-few is marginally higher (69.69% vs 69.63%), and zero-shot has the lowest CFACT rate for every backbone. Method proposed in the paper

Scope. This estimates accessible knowledge under a particular search procedure. It needs target answers and model gradients, and semantic constraints do not guarantee meaning preservation or exhaustive coverage. Read the study ↗

Research summary

Fixed prompts can underestimate the knowledge that a language model can express. We define a knowledge boundary that includes both prompt-agnostic and prompt-sensitive knowledge, and introduce projected gradient descent with semantic constraints (PGDC) to search for prompts that elicit known answers. Experiments compare elicitation success, robustness on fabricated knowledge, and human judgments of semantic preservation. The resulting estimate characterizes accessible knowledge while retaining limitations from the search procedure and imperfect semantic constraints.
